name: Istio
tagline: Four Kubernetes clusters, one mesh: shared trust, an istiod and a cluster gateway in each.

howItWorks.title: What it is and where it sits
howItWorks.body:
Istio adds a programmable proxy layer beside every workload, so apps need no code changes.
It works at L4 for mTLS and TCP policy, and L7 for HTTP and gRPC routing.
Here it joins four Kubernetes clusters into one mesh: a service in cluster A calls a service in cluster D by its normal name.
It sits above the Kubernetes Services and below your edge proxy (HAProxy or NGINX with a floating address).

howItWorks.title: Components and architecture
howItWorks.body:
Shared root CA: one root of trust; each cluster gets its own intermediate CA signed by it.
istiod (control plane), one per cluster: issues workload certificates, pushes routes and policy, and reads the other clusters' Services.
Pods with an Envoy sidecar (data plane): enforce routes and mTLS on every call, in this cluster or another.
Cluster gateway (data plane), one per cluster: an Envoy pod that lets the other clusters' sidecars reach Services here.
NodePort Service, one per cluster: exposes the cluster gateway on every node. A load balancer or VIP in front is optional.

howItWorks.title: Four clusters, one mesh
howItWorks.body:
Install Istio in every cluster with the same mesh ID and one shared root CA; each cluster keeps its own istiod.
Each istiod issues SPIFFE certificates from an intermediate CA signed by the common root, so a workload in cluster A can prove its identity to cluster D.
Each istiod reads the other clusters' Services through a remote secret, so every sidecar knows every endpoint in all four clusters.
A call to a Service in another cluster leaves through the local sidecar, reaches the peer's gateway pod on port 18443, and stays mTLS from sidecar to sidecar.
The gateway uses SNI passthrough: it routes by server name and never decrypts the traffic.
Every pair of clusters connects both ways; the diagram draws one direction per pair to stay readable.

howItWorks.title: Control plane and data plane
howItWorks.body:
The control plane is istiod: it issues workload certificates, pushes routes and policy, and watches the Kubernetes API. Each cluster in the diagram has its own.
The data plane is every Envoy that carries traffic: the sidecar next to each app on the worker nodes, and the gateway pods at the edge.
If a control plane goes down, running proxies keep their last configuration and keep serving traffic; only new config and new certificates wait.
The control plane never sits in the request path; the data plane does, so size and scale gateways, not istiod, for throughput.

howItWorks.title: What topology.istio.io/network does
howItWorks.body:
It is a label that names the network a workload lives on, for example topology.istio.io/network=network-a on the istio-system namespace and on the gateway.
Istio compares networks: an endpoint on the same network is reached directly by its pod IP; an endpoint on another network is reached through that network's gateway.
With four clusters on four separate networks, give each its own value (network-a to network-d) so sidecars know when a peer needs the gateway path.
Two clusters with the same network label are treated as one flat network: pod IPs must be routable between them and no gateway is used.
Set the matching network when you install Istio, and tell Istio the address peers should use for each network's gateway.

howItWorks.title: Kinds of gateway
howItWorks.body:
Ingress gateway: an Envoy pod at the mesh edge for traffic entering from outside (north-south). A Gateway resource opens ports and hosts; a VirtualService routes them.
Egress gateway: an Envoy pod that traffic leaves through to external hosts, so exit traffic can be controlled and audited from one place.
Cluster gateway (the one in the four-cluster diagram): an Envoy pod that exposes port 18443 so sidecars in other clusters can reach Services here. It uses SNI passthrough, so mTLS stays end to end.
A gateway is either defined with the Istio Gateway resource, which selects a gateway pod, or with the Kubernetes Gateway API, where Istio creates the pod for you.
In ambient mode the equivalent roles are played by waypoint proxies and a gateway per network.

howItWorks.title: Flat network or separate networks?
howItWorks.body:
Flat network (one network): pod IPs are routable between all clusters, so sidecars call remote pods directly. No gateway hop, but pod CIDRs must not overlap and the network must route them, usually with a VPN, BGP or a shared CNI fabric.
Separate networks (multi-network): clusters need not route pod IPs; traffic crosses through each cluster's gateway. Pod CIDRs may overlap, at the cost of one extra hop and gateways to scale.
Control plane: multi-primary runs an istiod in every cluster, so each cluster survives alone. Primary-remote runs istiod in one or two clusters and the others use it: fewer istiods, but those clusters depend on it for new config.
For four clusters a common choice is multi-primary on separate networks. Choose a flat network only when the clusters genuinely share one routable fabric.
Either way: one mesh ID, one shared root CA, a unique cluster name per cluster, and API access between clusters for endpoint discovery.

howItWorks.title: Load balancer or NodePort?
howItWorks.body:
NodePort plus the gateway pod is enough when the clusters share a private network: peers dial any node IP on the NodePort and kube-proxy hands the connection to the gateway pod.
Add a load balancer or VIP (MetalLB, HAProxy with VRRP, or a cloud load balancer) when node IPs change, a node can disappear, or a firewall rule wants one stable address per cluster.
A load balancer here must be plain TCP passthrough on the gateway port; terminating TLS on it breaks cross-cluster mTLS.
With four clusters you need at most four addresses, one per cluster, never one balancer in front of all four.
Tell Istio which address peers should use for each cluster's gateway, and list two or more nodes so one failure does not cut a cluster off.

howItWorks.title: Request flow
howItWorks.body:
The app calls a Service name as usual; the local sidecar intercepts the outbound connection.
Envoy matches the host against VirtualService rules and picks a destination; endpoints from all four clusters are candidates.
A local endpoint is called directly. A remote one is called through that cluster's gateway: the sidecar opens mTLS to the NodePort address and the gateway passes it through untouched.
The remote sidecar checks the caller's certificate and AuthorizationPolicy, then hands the request to the app.
From outside the mesh, traffic enters through the ingress gateway behind your edge proxy, then follows the same path.

howItWorks.title: Configuration model
howItWorks.body:
Gateway opens ports and hosts at the edge; VirtualService binds routes to it or to mesh traffic.
DestinationRule defines subsets by pod label plus traffic policy; apply it before weighted routes. A subset can span clusters: version v1 in A and v2 in B is a cross-cluster canary.
A Service with the same name and namespace in several clusters is one logical service; keep namespaces identical.
meshNetworks maps each network to the address and port of its cluster gateway (the NodePort); the network label says which network a workload is on.
PeerAuthentication sets mTLS (STRICT or PERMISSIVE); AuthorizationPolicy allows or denies by identity and is evaluated on the receiving sidecar.

howItWorks.title: Connecting to its neighbours
howItWorks.body:
In front (Edge): your edge proxy (HAProxy or NGINX with a floating address) forwards to the ingress gateway Service, usually a NodePort on bare metal.
Beside (the other clusters): each cluster's cluster gateway, reached on a NodePort or a VIP; each istiod also needs to reach every peer's Kubernetes API for discovery.
Behind (Platform): sidecars route to Kubernetes Services and pods using the VirtualService and DestinationRule rules.
Beside (Operators): Prometheus and Grafana consume mesh metrics from every cluster.

howItWorks.title: Security
howItWorks.body:
One root CA signs every cluster's intermediate CA, so a certificate from any cluster verifies in all four. Clusters with different roots cannot talk.
istiod issues short-lived workload certificates; rotation is automatic. The trust domain stays the same across clusters, so identities such as cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/frontend mean the same thing everywhere.
PERMISSIVE accepts plaintext and mTLS; STRICT demands mTLS. Migrate in that order, mesh-wide in istio-system once every client is meshed.
AuthorizationPolicy is default-allow until an ALLOW policy selects a workload; then deny the rest. Cross-cluster callers are matched by the same principals.
The cluster gateway never decrypts cross-cluster traffic, so a compromised gateway pod cannot read it.

howItWorks.title: Resilience, HA and scaling
howItWorks.body:
Multi-primary means each cluster has its own istiod; a cluster keeps working if the other three are down. Run two or more istiod replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget.
Proxies keep their last config if istiod is down; only new config and new certificates wait.
Outlier detection ejects a failing endpoint, local or remote, so traffic shifts to healthy clusters.
Scale cluster gateways with replicas and spread them across nodes; the gateway, not istiod, carries cross-cluster throughput.
A VIP (VRRP or MetalLB) per cluster gives peers one healthy address; without it, list two or more node addresses.

howItWorks.title: Observability
howItWorks.body:
Every sidecar emits request count, duration and size metrics for Prometheus, tagged with source and destination cluster.
Access logs and Envoy tracing headers feed Grafana, Jaeger or Tempo and Kiali across all four clusters.
Golden signals come free per workload without touching application code.
Alert on 5xx rate and request p95 per destination service, and on proxies not SYNCED or a peer cluster not synced.

howItWorks.title: Failure modes and troubleshooting
howItWorks.body:
istioctl analyze finds config errors before they cause failures.
istioctl remote-clusters shows whether each peer's remote secret is synced; a missing peer means no endpoints from that cluster.
istioctl proxy-status shows which proxies are STALE or not SYNCED with istiod.
503 with NR means no route; UH means no healthy upstream; UF is upstream connection failure. A remote cluster that is only reachable through a blocked NodePort shows as UF.
Certificate errors across clusters almost always mean the clusters do not share one root CA, or the clocks differ.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
Linkerd: choose it for a smaller, simpler mesh with automatic mTLS and multi-cluster via service mirroring.
Cilium Cluster Mesh: choose it for an eBPF data plane and a flat pod network across clusters.
Consul: choose it when VMs and Kubernetes share one mesh.
No mesh: Kubernetes Services plus Ingress are enough when you do not need mTLS or traffic splitting between clusters.

flow: The client calls the Service name as normal.
The sidecar intercepts the outbound connection through iptables redirect.
Envoy matches the host and picks a destination from endpoints in all four clusters.
A local endpoint is called directly; a remote one goes through that cluster's gateway.
The sidecar opens mTLS to the NodePort address of the peer's cluster gateway.
The gateway passes the encrypted stream through to the right Service, using the TLS server name.
The remote sidecar verifies the certificate chain back to the shared root CA.
The remote sidecar checks AuthorizationPolicy and forwards to the app.

deploy.summary: Join four clusters into one mesh: shared root CA, istiod and a cluster gateway on a NodePort in each, then verify.
prerequisites: Four Kubernetes clusters with kubectl contexts, for example ctx-a, ctx-b, ctx-c and ctx-d
Node addresses of every cluster reachable from the others on the NodePort range
Each istiod able to reach the other clusters' API servers (port 6443) for discovery
Placeholders in <angle brackets> are yours to set

steps.title: Create one shared root CA and an intermediate per cluster
steps.code:
curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | ISTIO_VERSION=1.24.1 sh -
cd istio-1.24.1 && export PATH=$PWD/bin:$PATH
mkdir -p certs && cd certs
make -f ../tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk root-ca
for c in a b c d; do make -f ../tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk cluster-$c-cacerts; done
steps.note: Keep the root key offline. Every cluster must be signed by the same root, or cross-cluster mTLS cannot work.

steps.title: Create the cacerts secret and the network label in each cluster
steps.code:
for c in a b c d; do
  kubectl --context ctx-$c create namespace istio-system
  kubectl --context ctx-$c create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system \
    --from-file=cluster-$c/ca-cert.pem --from-file=cluster-$c/ca-key.pem \
    --from-file=cluster-$c/root-cert.pem --from-file=cluster-$c/cert-chain.pem
  kubectl --context ctx-$c label namespace istio-system topology.istio.io/network=network-$c
done
steps.note: Create the secret before installing Istio, or each cluster generates its own root. The label names the cluster's network.

steps.title: Install Istio in each cluster (multi-primary, separate networks)
steps.code:
# cluster-a.yaml (repeat per cluster: cluster-b/network-b, and so on)
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  values:
    global:
      meshID: mesh1
      multiCluster:
        clusterName: cluster-a
      network: network-a

# istioctl install --context ctx-a -f cluster-a.yaml -y
steps.note: One meshID for all four, a unique clusterName and network for each. Pods must show the istiod running in every cluster.

steps.title: Add the cluster gateway on a NodePort in each cluster
steps.code:
# gateway deployment labelled with the network, service type NodePort
# listener port <GW_PORT> (for example 18443), nodePort <NODE_PORT> (for example 31843)
kubectl --context ctx-a -n istio-system get svc istio-clustergateway
# then apply a Gateway on selector istio=clustergateway: a TLS server on <GW_PORT>,
# passthrough mode, hosts *.local
steps.note: The gateway pod only passes encrypted traffic through. Label it with topology.istio.io/network=network-a, then repeat in B, C and D.

steps.title: Tell each cluster where the other networks' gateways are
steps.code:
# in cluster A's mesh config (repeat for B, C and D, listing the other three)
meshNetworks:
  network-b:
    endpoints: [{fromRegistry: cluster-b}]
    gateways: [{address: <NODE_IP_B>, port: <NODE_PORT>}]
  network-c:
    endpoints: [{fromRegistry: cluster-c}]
    gateways: [{address: <NODE_IP_C>, port: <NODE_PORT>}]
  network-d:
    endpoints: [{fromRegistry: cluster-d}]
    gateways: [{address: <NODE_IP_D>, port: <NODE_PORT>}]
steps.note: With a VIP in front of the NodePort, use the VIP as the address. Without one, a node address works but does not follow node failures.

steps.title: Exchange remote secrets so every istiod discovers every peer
steps.code:
for from in a b c d; do for to in a b c d; do
  [ $from = $to ] && continue
  istioctl create-remote-secret --context ctx-$from --name cluster-$from |
    kubectl apply -f - --context ctx-$to
done; done
istioctl remote-clusters --context ctx-a
steps.note: Twelve secrets for four clusters: each cluster reads the other three. The last command lists each peer as synced.

steps.title: Test a call across clusters
steps.code:
for c in a b c d; do kubectl --context ctx-$c create namespace sample
  kubectl --context ctx-$c label namespace sample istio-injection=enabled; done
# helloworld v1 in cluster A, v2 in cluster B; sleep client in cluster A
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl --context ctx-a -n sample exec deploy/sleep -c sleep -- curl -sS helloworld.sample:5000/hello
done
steps.note: Replies alternate between v1 and v2: the second one came from another cluster, through its gateway, over mTLS.

steps.title: Weighted routing across clusters
steps.note: Apply the DestinationRule first. A subset spans clusters, so v1 in A and v2 in B is a cross-cluster canary.

steps.title: STRICT mTLS across the mesh
steps.note: Apply it in every cluster once all clients are meshed. Plaintext callers are reset, and so are other clusters' sidecars without certificates.

verify: istioctl analyze -A reports no issues in each cluster.
istioctl remote-clusters --context ctx-a lists cluster-b, cluster-c and cluster-d as synced.
istioctl proxy-status shows every proxy SYNCED in every cluster.
Calls to helloworld alternate between v1 and v2 across clusters.
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> shows the same root certificate in all four clusters.
pitfalls: Clusters with different root CAs cannot establish cross-cluster mTLS; create cacerts before installing Istio.
A duplicate clusterName or a missing network label makes remote endpoints invisible or misrouted.
A remote secret that is missing or blocked by the firewall means no endpoints from that cluster.
A load balancer that terminates TLS in front of the cluster gateway breaks cross-cluster mTLS.
Peers cannot reach a NodePort that a firewall blocks; open the NodePort range between the clusters.
A meshNetworks port that does not match the gateway NodePort fails with upstream connection errors.
Clock skew between clusters invalidates short-lived certificates.
A missing subset in the DestinationRule returns 503 with NR or UH response flags.
Enabling STRICT before every client is meshed resets plaintext callers.
Default retries plus your own retries multiply load; set attempts explicitly.
keyPoints: One shared root CA lets any cluster verify any other cluster's certificates.
Each cluster runs its own istiod (control plane); the sidecars and gateways are the data plane.
The cluster gateway passes mTLS through; NodePort plus the gateway is enough on a private network.
The network label tells Istio whether a peer is reached directly or through its gateway.
VirtualService and DestinationRule subsets drive canary and blue-green, even across clusters.
quickDeploy: Create one root CA and a cacerts secret per cluster.
Install Istio in each cluster with the same meshID and its own clusterName and network.
Add a cluster gateway on a NodePort, and list the peers in meshNetworks.
Exchange remote secrets, then test with helloworld across clusters.
osiNote: mTLS and TCP passthrough at L4; HTTP and gRPC routing at L7.
production: Run multi-primary: an istiod in every cluster, with two or more replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget.
Use one mesh ID and one shared root CA across all clusters; give each its own intermediate CA and keep the root offline.
Put a VIP (VRRP or MetalLB) in front of each cluster gateway, or list two or more node addresses.
Pin the Istio version; upgrade with revisions, one cluster at a time, and canary the data plane.
Set explicit timeouts, retries and outlier detection on every hot route.
Keep PERMISSIVE until every client is meshed, then enforce STRICT.
Alert on 5xx rate, request p95, proxies not SYNCED and a peer cluster not synced.
